The electricity from the plug-in outlet is consumed by any devices connected on the same circuit first. Any excessive electricity is fed to the circuit breaker panel’s bar connecting all circuits on the same 120V split phase; the devices connected the the circuits on the same split phase can use the plug-in electricity next. Any excessive electricity is fed back out of the meter on the 120V split phase line on your main service connection, then to the electric company’s transformer at the street block. The transformer might feed it to your neighbors. In any case the transformer feed electricity to the other 120V split phase line back into your service connection, the meter, the panel, the other split phase bar, the circuits on it, and the outlets on them. The devices on the other split phase circuits technically are not using the plug-in power.

Most modern meters will debit and credit the electricity going in and out on both split phase lines as net meter, so the electricity consumed in the other split phase is counted as consuming the plug-in power. However some old meters add the outgoing electricity up as consumption so you are paying for the electricity fed into the grid. Call your utility company to make sure.

Also, unless you have a net metering agreement with your utility company, you won’t get paid for any excessive electricity fed back into the grid.

Three-phase power is really about delivering more power with less copper by 1) sharing the neutral conductor (or getting rid of it) and 2) using lower currents which can make do with much thinner conductors.

The difference between one three-phase feeder and three completely separate two-wire circuits is that the three phases, which are 120° apart, share a single neutral conductor. In fact, if the load is perfectly balanced across the phases and currents are sine waves, they will cancel each other out, so neutral will carry no current at all and can be omitted! But in practice, there still usually is a neutral conductor to carry the imbalance (except for specific loads like delta and star motors under certain conditions). In total, we only need 4 wires instead of 6 to carry the same amount of power. That's 1/3 less copper! (Excluding PE of course.)

Now, compared to using a single two-wire circuit rated for three times the current, three-phase also wins by a long shot. (We're again assuming a balanced load and equal power factors.) This is because resistive heat scales with the current squared, so 3 times the current produces 9 times the amount of heat at the same resistance. So, we need to use thicker conductors to lower the resistance. But the area of its cross-section grows quicker than the surface area to dissipate heat, so the maximum current a conductor can safely carry scales sublinearly with its cross-sectional area. For example, 1.5mm² will suffice under most conditions to carry 16A, but for 48A we'll typically need 10mm².

All in all, the rule of thumb is that three-phase AC gets you the same amount of power for roughly 25% less copper compared to single-phase AC!

Some loads also make use of the rotating magnetic field, like motors (see below).

Lastly, lower currents will reduce heating in case of loose connections, reducing the risk of fire. On the other hand, a 400V RMS phase-to-phase shock is a lot more severe than a 230V RMS phase-to-neutral (or phase-to-PE) shock.

Common use cases (load-side):

- Motors. Three phases produce a rotating magnetic field, perfect for simple self-starting motors. (Arguably, this is less relevant today with more modern motor designs, though three-phase induction motors are still widely used.)

- Electric cookers (usually split by cooking zones and oven, like one phase for two zones each, and the third phase for the oven)

- Water heaters (especially those that heat water instantaneously on demand)

- EV charging (even an ancient European three-phase installation is likely able to deliver 11kW of power and can therefore fully charge an EV overnight)

The floating point values were valid, they were stored in the text files (unknowingly) in a locale dependent way, either by having a program use a locale sensitive functions to write the values, or because the values were written by hand using the developer's native way of number formatting. The values were then read using the locale dependent functions (like strtod) and if run on a machine with a locale that formatted numbers differently (i.e. using comma for decimal separator) they would return incorrect values.

This caused issues in the game as the values would be significantly different than originally designed, and it would be hard to test for since the people testing the game would usually be using a similar locale to the developer writing the game, and therefore they would only become apparent upon release or wider testing. Now the fix was to explicitly specify the locale before reading the data files, but it still took time to find and implement the fix.
